query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding trace amounts of yttrium to the refractory high-entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a stable, adherent oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) currently used in extreme-temperature structural applications without any reactive element addition.
generation.intervention: Introduce trace amounts (e.g., on the order of 0.1–0.5 wt%) of yttrium into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1100°C for 100 hours in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (e.g., ambient air or pure oxygen) to simulate prolonged high-temperature service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale (potentially incorporating yttrium oxides) on the alloy surface, which acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: Yttrium segregates to the oxide grain boundaries during high-temperature exposure, enhancing the adhesion and stability of a protective scale (similar to the reactive element effect seen in Ni-based superalloys) and thereby reducing the oxidation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: The yttrium-doped HEA will exhibit a significantly reduced oxidation rate (e.g., lower weight gain and thinner, more coherent oxide layers) relative to the untreated alloy under the same exposure conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory HEA exhibiting rapid oxidation and less adherent oxide scale formation under extreme-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under high-temperature (around 1100°C) oxygen or air exposure for prolonged periods (approximately 100 hours); outside these conditions, the effect may be less pronounced or require further investigation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the oxidation reduction (e.g., percentage decrease in weight gain) remains uncertain and may depend on the optimal yttrium concentration and alloy microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the refractory HEA: one set with the designated trace amount of yttrium added and a control set without yttrium. Expose both sets to 1100°C in air for 100 hours. After exposure, measure the oxidation weight gain, inspect the oxide scale thickness and adherence using microscopy, and evaluate the formation of any yttrium-enriched regions at the scale interfaces.
measurements: Scale adherence (via scratch tests or similar methods)
Elemental mapping of oxide scales (using EDS to identify yttrium segregation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the yttrium-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar or higher weight gain and comparable oxide scale characteristics) compared to the untreated alloy under the specified conditions.

frame.system: Refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) used for high-temperature structural applications in its conventional, untreated state.
frame.goal: To enhance the alloy’s high-temperature oxygen resistance, i.e. its ability to form a stable protective oxide scale and resist oxidation relative to the baseline alloy.
frame.limitation: The currently used refractory HEA exhibits inadequate high-temperature oxidation resistance under extreme-temperature conditions, compromising its structural integrity during prolonged exposure to oxidizing environments.
constraints: only a single intervention is allowed
the hypothesis must specify the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy
the operating conditions (temperature, atmosphere, exposure time) must be clearly defined
the proposal should cite supporting prior evidence
an experiment must be proposed that includes a definitive result which could falsify the hypothesis
frame.regime: Operating under extreme high-temperature conditions (e.g., around 1000–1200°C) in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (pure oxygen or air) for extended exposure durations (such as 100 hours or more) to simulate service conditions.
prior_attempts: Use of untreated refractory HEAs that lack tailored oxidation-resistant scales

Reactive element additions in conventional high-temperature alloys (e.g., yttrium in Ni-based superalloys) have been shown to improve oxidation resistance; however, such an approach has not been definitively implemented or optimized in refractory HEAs.

families.principle: Altering the alloy’s elemental makeup can activate the formation of a desired, self-healing protective oxide scale (via reactive element effects) that impedes oxygen ingress at high temperatures.
cues_for: reactive element additions in conventional high-temperature alloys have improved oxidation resistance
cues_against: the current untreated alloy does not have tailored oxidation‐scale forming chemistry
families.best_lever: Introduce trace amounts of a reactive element (e.g., yttrium) to the refractory HEA to promote the formation of a stable, adherent oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.

families.principle: Directly modifying the surface, such as by applying a coating or surface treatment, can produce an engineered protective oxide scale that resists degradation in oxygen-rich, high-temperature environments.
cues_for: the need to form a stable protective oxide scale
the refractory HEA in its untreated state lacks tailored surface properties for oxidation resistance
cues_against: potential concerns about maintaining bulk mechanical properties while modifying the surface
families.best_lever: Deposit a thin, adherent alumina-based or reactive-element-enhanced coating on the HEA surface to ensure rapid formation of a robust, protective oxide scale during operation.

families.principle: Adjusting synthesis parameters or processing environments can influence the initial formation and distribution of oxide-forming phases during alloy fabrication.
cues_for: the alloy is currently in a conventional, untreated state
cues_against: the question emphasizes a single intervention with clear mechanism on oxidation resistance rather than overall processing modifications
families.best_lever: Employ a controlled synthesis atmosphere (e.g., oxygen partial pressure tuning) to pre-form a protective oxide phase during material fabrication.

families.principle: Tailored heat treatments or thermomechanical protocols can modify the oxide scale formation kinetics and encourage the development of protective surface layers.
cues_for: focused high-temperature performance and oxidation behavior
cues_against: the need for a single intervention that directly targets the oxidation mechanism rather than altering bulk treatment protocols
families.best_lever: Apply a post-synthesis annealing treatment in a controlled oxygen atmosphere to induce in-situ formation of a protective oxide scale.

families.principle: Engineering the internal microstructure (e.g., grain boundaries and phase dispersion) can affect diffusion paths for oxygen and thus modify oxidation kinetics.
cues_for: the structural use under extreme-temperature conditions implies that mechanical integrity and diffusion barriers are important
cues_against: the question’s emphasis is on improving oxidation resistance via an intervention that promotes a stable protective oxide scale rather than microstructural diffusion barriers
families.best_lever: Develop a refined multiphase microstructure in which specific, oxidation‐resistant phases are positioned at grain boundaries to hinder oxygen ingress.
